questions.explanation: `runBlocking` runs on one thread with an event loop, so `launch` only queues the child and the parent keeps going and prints B. `yield()` suspends the parent and lets the queued child run, which prints A, and then the parent resumes and prints C. The child never runs before the parent suspends.

questions.question: A ViewModel sets `_state.value = UiState(loading = false)` twice in a row on a `MutableStateFlow` (UiState is a data class). How many times does an active collector receive it?
options: Twice, unless `distinctUntilChanged()` is added before `collect`
Zero times: StateFlow only emits when the value's reference changes
Once: StateFlow skips a new value that is equal to the current one
Twice: every assignment to value is delivered to every collector
questions.explanation: StateFlow is conflated and compares with `equals()`, so assigning an equal data class instance is a no-op. That is why `distinctUntilChanged()` on a StateFlow is redundant. If you need every event delivered, even equal ones, use a SharedFlow or a Channel instead.

upstream caught

got 1
got 2
outer caught

got 1
outer caught

got 1
upstream caught
got 2
questions.explanation: `catch` only handles exceptions from the operators above it; it cannot see an exception thrown in the `collect` block below it. So `check(it != 1)` throws IllegalStateException in the collector, the flow is cancelled and the exception reaches the outer `try`. That is why errors in collect logic are often moved into `onEach` placed before `catch`.

questions.question: Inside `coroutineScope { }` you start `val a = async { fetchA() }` and `val b = async { fetchB() }`. `fetchA()` throws an IOException before anyone calls `await()`. What happens?
options: `b` is cancelled, and `coroutineScope` throws the IOException to its caller once its children have finished
`b` keeps running, and the IOException is handed to the CoroutineExceptionHandler in the context
Nothing happens until `a.await()` is called, so `b` keeps running and its result can still be used
Only `a` fails; `coroutineScope` returns normally with `b`'s result because async isolates its failure
questions.explanation: In a regular scope a failing child cancels its parent, which cancels the siblings, and `coroutineScope` rethrows the failure. `async` stores the exception for `await()`, but it still propagates the failure through the job hierarchy right away. To keep `b` alive you would use `supervisorScope`, and then handle the exception at `a.await()`.

questions.question: Why would you wrap cleanup in `withContext(NonCancellable) { ... }` inside a `finally` block of a coroutine?
options: Without it the `finally` block is skipped completely when a coroutine is cancelled, so the cleanup never runs
It stops the parent scope from cancelling any other children while this coroutine is busy cleaning up
It moves the cleanup onto a background thread so a slow cleanup cannot block the main thread of the app
Once the coroutine is cancelled, any suspending call in `finally` throws CancellationException right away; NonCancellable lets the cleanup suspend and finish
questions.explanation: `finally` still runs on cancellation, but the coroutine's Job is already cancelled, so cancellable suspend functions (e.g. `delay`, a suspending DAO call) throw immediately. `NonCancellable` gives that block a Job that is never cancelled so cleanup such as 'mark upload as paused' completes. It does not change the dispatcher and should only wrap short cleanup work.

questions.question: Which statements about handling cancellation in coroutines are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A child failing with CancellationException makes its parent fail and cancels every sibling as a result
A `catch (e: Exception)` that does not rethrow CancellationException lets code continue after the coroutine was cancelled
Coroutines running on Dispatchers.IO ignore cancellation, so `cancel()` has no effect on blocking calls there
`runCatching { suspendingCall() }` also catches CancellationException, which can keep a cancelled coroutine running
Rethrowing CancellationException (or calling `ensureActive()` after catching) keeps cooperative cancellation working
questions.explanation: CancellationException is how cancellation is delivered, so swallowing it (often via broad catches or `runCatching`) breaks structured concurrency. A CancellationException is treated as normal cancellation, so it does not fail the parent. Dispatchers.IO coroutines are cancellable like any other, though a blocking Java call itself will not be interrupted unless you use something like `runInterruptible`.

questions.question: `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` changes the context of the operators before it (upstream), while the collector and the operators after it keep running in the collecting coroutine's context.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `flowOn` only affects upstream, which keeps context preservation intact: the collector always runs where `collect` was called. That is why you put `flowOn` right after the expensive producer and collect from the main thread. Inside a plain `flow { }` builder, using `withContext` to emit from another dispatcher is an error, and `flowOn` is the supported way.

sibling ok

caught x
done

sibling ok
caught x
done

caught x
sibling ok
done
questions.explanation: In `supervisorScope` a child failure does not cancel the scope or its siblings, and the failing child's own CoroutineExceptionHandler handles the exception, so 'caught x' prints first when the first child runs. The second child is unaffected and prints after its delay. `supervisorScope` waits for all children, then 'done' prints.

questions.question: Why is `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)` a common choice for UI state backed by a database or location flow?
options: It caches the last value for five seconds and then resets the StateFlow back to the initial value each time
It keeps the upstream alive through a short gap such as a rotation, but stops it a few seconds after the UI really goes away
It restarts the upstream every five seconds so the UI always shows data fresher than five seconds old
It delays the first collection by five seconds so the screen's first frame is drawn before any data loading begins
questions.explanation: During a configuration change the collector disappears for a moment and comes back; a short timeout avoids restarting an expensive upstream. When the app goes to the background, collection stops and after the timeout the upstream is cancelled, saving battery. The replay value is kept by default (the expiration parameter controls resetting), and nothing is delayed or polled.

questions.question: A repository guards a token refresh with `mutex.withLock { ... }`. Inside the block it calls a helper that also does `mutex.withLock { }` on the same Mutex. What happens?
options: The coroutine suspends forever: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex is not reentrant, so it waits on a lock it already holds
It throws IllegalStateException at once, because Mutex detects a nested lock by the same owner by default
It works, because Mutex is reentrant for the same coroutine just like a Java ReentrantLock is for a thread
It blocks the underlying thread until the outer block finishes, which then lets the inner block continue
questions.explanation: `Mutex` is non-reentrant; a nested `withLock` on the same instance suspends waiting for itself, which is a deadlock with no error. (Passing an `owner` to `lock` can turn a double lock by the same owner into an exception, but `withLock` without an owner does not.) Mutex suspends rather than blocking threads, so the fix is to restructure so the lock is taken once.
